unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: none of the admissible sources (NC State, MOBOT, Clemson, RHS) state any toxicity information for Rudbeckia fulgida to pets or people.
day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max: sources give USDA hardiness zones (NC State/MOBOT: zones 3-9; Clemson: zones 4-9) but no numeric ambient day/night temperature ranges.
chill_damage_f: not addressed by any admissible source.
cool_rest_note: not addressed; NC State notes a winter basal rosette persists as ground cover, but no dormancy/rest-temperature guidance is given.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max: outdoor garden perennial; no admissible source discusses ambient humidity requirements.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no source gives foot-candle values; light is described only in full-sun/partial-shade terms.
direct_sun_hours_max: NC State defines full sun as '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day' — a minimum threshold, not a stated maximum.
soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: RHS states pH tolerance categorically as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (i.e., broadly tolerant) but no source gives numeric pH bounds.

water_regime: MOBOT's structured field reads 'Water: Dry to medium' and RHS/NC State describe 'moist but well-drained' soil with drought tolerance once established, but no source frames watering as a surface-dry-between vs. deep-dry-between pattern, so mapping to one of the four enum values would be a guess.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source describes watering in these houseplant-style terms (soil-check depth, days between waterings) for this outdoor perennial.
fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule for Rudbeckia fulgida.

Container/patio use: RHS lists 'Patio and container plants' among suggested garden types for this species, alongside borders/beds/meadows/prairie plantings; since soil_base is single-valued and every source's primary cultivation description is outdoor garden soil, soil_base is recorded as garden_bed rather than a potting category. Clemson separately notes only specific cultivars ('City Garden', 'Little Goldstar') as 'ideal for container gardening,' not the species itself.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Record asserts 'moderate', but NC State's own page has an explicit structured attribute — 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist Occasionally Dry' (verified via live fetch of plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rudbeckia-fulgida/) — none of which is 'moderate.' Neither the NC State prose cited ('thriving in any but soggy soils') nor the RHS quote cited ('moist but well-drained') contains the word 'moderate' either. The researcher had a precise, directly quotable categorical field available on the cited source and instead inferred an unsupported term from vaguer prose.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note claims 'glowing coneflower' is used by both MOBOT and RHS. I fetched the cited RHS page (rhs.org.uk/plants/112261) directly and searched the full text: zero occurrences of 'glowing' or 'coneflower' anywhere on the page. Only MOBOT's common-names list actually contains 'glowing coneflower' (confirmed present: 'orange coneflower / black-eyed Susan / glowing coneflower'). The RHS attribution is fabricated, and no citation in the array supports the 'glowing coneflower' claim for either source.

soil_base — removed on audit: The record picks the single value 'garden_bed' despite acknowledging in unknowns that RHS lists 'Patio and container plants' among suggested garden types (confirmed via live fetch: 'Cottage and informal garden, Patio and container plants, Wildlife gardens, Wildflower meadow, Prairie planting, Cut flowers, Flower borders and beds') and Clemson names two R. fulgida cultivars as container-ideal. This is a real cross-source signal resolved by picking a side rather than reflecting the ambiguity. Additionally, citation 9 is labeled as supporting 'soil_base garden_bed' but its quoted text ('Grow in humus rich, moist but well-drained soil...') only describes soil texture, not bed/placement usage — the label overclaims what the quote shows.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good: none of the admissible extension/garden sources for this outdoor hardy perennial give indoor humidity percentages or foot-candle light readings.

soil_base — removed on audit: The citation supporting soil_base='garden_bed' quotes MoBot's 'rhizomatous spread in beds and borders can pose significant problems of control and removal' -- but in full context this sentence is a caution about invasive spread, not a statement that the plant is grown in beds/borders. MoBot's own Uses section (not cited) states the opposite directly: 'Not recommended for beds or borders where the spreading rhizomes can be difficult to remove,' recommending 'Naturalized areas or cottage gardens' instead, and the page banner even reads 'Midwest Noxious Weed: Do Not Plant.' The citation's parenthetical '(grown outdoors in garden beds and borders)' reframes a warning as an endorsement, misrepresenting what the source actually says.

toxicity_detail — nulled on landing review: the field was populated with human/livestock toxicology content (NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block: severity, toxic part, 'can be fatal in large quantities'; horse/cow toxicity; contact dermatitis) even though the record correctly left toxic_to_pets null for lacking any cat/dog/companion-pet-specific evidence. This is the human/pet blending pattern the b14 rule targets, just moved into the detail field instead of the boolean -- toxicity_detail is the pet-facing companion to toxic_to_pets and should stay null alongside it. The underlying reasoning is preserved in the unknowns entry above.

unknowns: direct_sun_hours_max: NC State gives only a floor for full sun ('6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day') with no stated upper bound.

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: NC State and RHS both give only categorical pH tolerance bins ('Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' at NC State; 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' at RHS), not a continuous numeric range stated for this species -- no defensible single min/max number is quotable.
water_dry_down_target: no admissible source states a specific dry-down checkpoint before rewatering.
water_check_depth_cm: no admissible source gives a moisture-check depth.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a day-interval watering frequency for Viola cornuta specifically; the only day-interval watering language found (Clemson HGIC factsheet 'Pansies and Johnny-Jump-Ups') is written under the heading for Pansies (Viola x wittrockiana), a separate section from that same page's Viola cornuta-labeled 'Johnny-Jump-Ups' entry, so it is not confidently attributable to this species.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: same source-attribution gap -- Clemson's fertilizer schedule ('Pansies grow best with a soil pH of 5.4 to 5.8...apply a 5-10-10 granular fertilizer in late fall and again in early spring') is stated under the Pansies heading, not the Viola cornuta-labeled Johnny-Jump-Ups section of that page.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source states an ambient humidity requirement for this outdoor garden plant.
light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light measurements; all light guidance found is stated as sun/shade exposure categories, not measured light levels.

day_f_min / day_f_max / night_f_min / night_f_max: no admissible source gives day/night operating-temperature targets; the only temperature-related data found are a USDA hardiness zone range (NC State/MBG) and an RHS winter-hardiness letter rating (H5), neither of which states a day/night temperature range.

chill_damage_f: RHS rates the species H5 ('hardy in most places throughout the UK even in severe winters (-15 to -10)' degrees C) but that is a coarse UK-regional hardiness band, not a stated species-specific damage threshold; converting the band's endpoint to one Fahrenheit number would require interpretation beyond the source's own wording.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source describes a dormancy or cool-rest requirement for this species.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: no admissible source assesses pet toxicity for Viola cornuta. NC State notes 'Flowers and leaves are edible' under its 'Edibility' field, but that is a human-edibility claim in a section distinct from any toxicity assessment, not a pet-safety determination, so it was not used to fill a pet-facing field.

Clemson HGIC's 'Pansies, Violas, and Panolas' article and UGA CAES's 'Violas best choice for coloring winter landscape' both use the common name 'viola' but explicitly attach it to Viola tricolor ('viola flowers (Viola tricolor)'; 'The viola is closer to Georgia's native plant species, viola tricolor'), so their care claims (fertilizing every 2-3 weeks, cold tolerance to below 0F, etc.) were excluded from this Viola cornuta record despite surface name overlap.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value is "moderate", but every quote attached to it says otherwise: NC State's structured tag reads "Good Drainage" (with a separate "Moist" tag, confirmed live on plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/viola-cornuta/), RHS's Moisture field reads "Moist but well–drained" (confirmed live on rhs.org.uk), and MBG's culture text reads "evenly moist, well-drained soils" (confirmed live on plantfinder.mobot.org). None of the three sources uses the word "moderate" or anything synonymous with it — "well-drained"/"Good Drainage" is a distinct, stronger drainage rating, and pairing it with "moist" describes a moisture-retention property, not a drainage-rate downgrade. This is not a one-off judgment call: it is the single most frequently reverted defect in this exact repository's own audit history — the identical "well-drained (+moist) mapped to moderate" pattern was caught and nulled across at least ten prior verified batches (app/data/verified/b5, b6, b7, b8, b9, b11, b12, b13, b14, b16, b17), each time citing the same "the quote says well-drained/Good Drainage, not moderate" reasoning. Most directly on point: the Pansy record (Viola × wittrockiana, the closest sibling species) in the very same b14-annual-flowers2.json batch had soil_drainage removed on audit for word-for-word the same NC State "consistently moist and well-drained" / structured "Good Drainage"/"Moist" tag pattern, with the note "'Good Drainage' does not map to 'moderate'". Per that established precedent this field should be null (the ambiguous well-drained+moist combination doesn't map cleanly to fast/moderate/moisture_retentive), not asserted as 'moderate'.

normalizations: 2026-08-21: the final batch of this collection run. Two fixes before landing. Horned Violet's first pass returned an empty citations array while still asserting four field values -- the same defect class as b17's Poppy -- recovered with a cheap single-species retry (299K tokens) rather than losing the work; the retry additionally caught a source-attribution ambiguity worth keeping in mind for future batches: Clemson's watering/fertilizing schedule was written under a 'Pansies' heading on a page that separately covers Viola cornuta under 'Johnny-Jump-Ups', and the record correctly declined to assume data under one species heading on a shared page applies to a different heading on the same page.

Tansy's toxicity_detail was nulled on landing review -- it held substantial human/livestock toxicology content (NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block, horse/cow toxicity, contact dermatitis) even though the record had correctly left toxic_to_pets null for lacking any cat/dog-specific evidence. Same human/pet blending pattern the b14 rule targets, just moved into the detail field instead of the boolean; the underlying reasoning is preserved in unknowns.

Rudbeckia's audit caught something more serious than the usual prose-vs-structured-data overreach: a fabricated citation attribution. The record's name_note claimed 'glowing coneflower' was used by both Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS; the audit fetched the cited RHS page directly and found zero occurrences of 'glowing' or 'coneflower' anywhere on it. Only MOBOT actually uses that name. Caught by direct verification against the live page rather than trusting the researcher's claim about what a source says -- which is the discipline this whole pipeline depends on.
